newsitem.title: MOROCCO: King Hassan sets October for new parliament session.
newsitem.headline: King Hassan sets October for new parliament session.

text.p: King Hassan said on Monday he wanted to see Morocco's new two-chamber parliament hold its inaugural session next October.

Giving his annual Throne Speech in a televised broadcast, the king said: "Determined as we are to proceed, with God's help, to the opening of the first session of the new parliament next October, it is envisaged that the first part of the electoral operation, which will be launched at national level, takes place before the end of May this year."

King Hassan gave no details as to what this "first part of the electoral operation" would be. Morocco is expecting new elections for regional council, chambers of industry and commerce and legislative elections.

The legislative poll will be for a bi-cameral parliament being created following a referendum last September 13. The existing 333-seat parliament is to be divided into a lower house and an upper house.

The first will be directly elected with the upper house, with power to bring down the government through a no-confidence vote. It will be indirectly elected through professional bodies, regional councils and trades unions.
King Hassan, in his hour-long speech, described the constitutional changes as being part of moves to strengthen democracy and modernise the country's institutions.
"In giving today to all active and productive forces more of a voice, we have wanted to mark clearly our option for the 'development' dimension of democracy...," he said.

Morocco had been engaged in a series of reforms in the past year which would be maintained, the king said. Already it had brought a high level of growth, resumption of tourism, a drop in the trade deficit, inflation and urban unemployment.
He said the most pleasing result had been in the North African country's record cereal harvest -- 10 million tonnes last year after only 1.6 million the year before following a catastrophic drought.

"We must not forget, that the four or five next years will be decisive for the future of Morocco if it wants to win the gamble of economic and social emergence in a definitive and irreversible fashion," King Hassan said.

Agreements signed last year with the European Union -- for a free trade zone excluding agriculture by the year 2009 -- could be decisive for the modernisation of Morocco's economic potential, he said.

But he also said North African countries, members of the Arab Maghreb Union (AMU), had no alterative but to cooperation or "soon find themselves on the margin of an international context dominated essentially by economic unions and scientific networks."

The five nation AMU was set up in 1989 with the aim of forging a strong economic bloc. But political differences among members - Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Libya, Mauritania -- have undermined any real progress to this.
One of these factors was a dispute between the Algerian- backed Polisario Front, seeking autonomy in the Western Sahara which is claimed and largely controlled by Morocco.
King Hassan accused the Polisario of "procrastination, prevarication and obstinacy" which had caused the failure of any final settlement.
